name: Abayomi Kehinde
feedback: D1 is a strong, evidence-led catalogue. You found all ten core findings plus two defensible extras (CSRF, role-from-JWT), and every row carries a quoted source line or a capture timestamp, which is exactly the standard. SQL injection at lines 64-67, alg:none at 48-50, the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret at line 30, the no-exp comment at 74-75, the stored XSS beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47, and the path traversal returning root:x:0:0 at 02:24:02 are all nailed. Two CWE choices drift (MD5 is fine as CWE-327 even though CWE-916 is the cleaner fit, and you put alg:none under A03 when it is really A07 auth failure), but the evidence lines are right so I credited them. Where D1 loses ground is the decoy. You disproved iat, and your reasoning that iat is inert and the real bug is the missing exp is internally sound, but iat was not the designated safe construct. The intended decoy is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and genuinely sound, so the tempting move was to flag it and the proof was to show the timing-safe comparison defeats that. You did not engage that construct, so that row stays low. To be clear, this is a miss and not fabrication; you never invented an exploit or rated a safe thing Critical, which is why there is no penalty. D2 is your weakest deliverable. The hops you wrote up (SQLi at 02:15:31, session at 02:15:33, the 312-row pull at 02:16:04, then the export) are reconciled verbatim to the capture and your PoC strings match the artefact. The problem is the chain stops short: you dropped the stored XSS at 02:18:47, the open redirect at 02:21:13, and the file read at 02:24:02 out of the D2 narrative entirely, and you never anchored the recon at 02:14:08 or the failed guess at 02:14:55. A full exploit chain has to walk every hop in order, so half the chain points are gone. Your SQLi CVSS vector is complete and well justified, but you set A:H when the bypass does not touch availability; the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N for about 9.1, not 9.8. You did capture the scope change on the export as S:C, which is the senior insight, good. The impact section is genuinely excellent: 312 customers, the ₦6,400 to ₦950,000 range, the ₦200,000 average stated as an assumption, ₦62.4M total, and the BoltCash six-week clock all land. D3 is the standout. The executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model names the external actor and the shared /api/v1/internal service, all twelve findings are tied to evidence, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort-to-risk and not by CVSS, with the 2-hour SQL parameterisation first and 2-day MD5 rehashing last, defended as highest risk reduction per hour. Your two stopgaps give exact ModSecurity rules on ARGS:username and ARGS:path with a stated sub-1 percent false-positive rate and a reason. The only soft spot in D3 is repeating the iat decoy instead of the hash_equals one. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon IV by number, anchors the decision to the SQLi you found at lines 64-67 and the 312 rows you counted yourself, and triggers the NDPA breach duty with the 72-hour NDPC clock and the high-risk data-subject notification. The one gap is that you named the duties but not the sections, so cite section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 affected data subjects. The single most important fix is to complete the D2 exploit chain so it walks every captured hop in order from recon at 02:14:08 through the file read at 02:24:02, because a half-chain undersells an intrusion you otherwise reconstructed very well.
